intro: Drive Mad is a physics driving game with two inputs. Your car sits at the left of a short course; accelerating pushes it over whatever is in the way, and braking or reversing lets you back off and try again. The cars are top-heavy and the courses are built to flip them, so the real skill is throttle control: too much speed over a ramp and you land on the roof, too little and you stall on the climb.

Every level is a self-contained gadget: seesaws, loops, breakable bridges, launchers, sometimes a car that changes shape mid-level. Reaching the flag unlocks the next level, and the level picker lets you jump back to any you have cleared. It is made in Fancade, so it plays identically in the browser and in the Fancade app.
DRIVE MAD.howTo: Feather the accelerator instead of holding it; most flips come from carrying speed into a ramp you did not need to take fast. If the car tips backwards, tap reverse to bring the nose down. When a level looks impossible, watch what the machinery does once before committing, since many of them have a timing window.
DRIVE MAD.controls: Desktop: right arrow or D to accelerate, left arrow or A to brake and reverse. Touch screens: tap and hold the right or left side of the screen.

intro: Red Ball 4 is a physics platformer where you are a rolling ball rather than a running character, and that changes everything about how it plays. You build momentum by rolling, you squash and stretch on impact, and you cannot stop on a sixpence — most deaths come from carrying speed into something rather than from failing a jump.

The hazard set is broad and specific: thorns, hammer presses that come down on a timer, electric traps, conveyors that fight your momentum, ladders to climb, and a battering-ram box and a ninja box among the objects you have to push, ride or avoid. Checkpoints are placed through each level so a mistake costs seconds rather than the stage.

It also has proper boss fights, which is unusual for the genre and is the part the game is remembered for. There is a four-category achievement system tracking the rest. Red Ball 4 was made by Yohoho Games.
Red Ball 4.howTo: Control your speed before an obstacle rather than during it, because a rolling ball has almost no air control once it has committed. Use the squash on landing as a timing cue for the next jump — the rebound is consistent, and chaining off it clears gaps a standing jump will not. On bosses, learn the pattern from a distance for one full cycle before trying to do damage; they all telegraph, and the arena is usually the bigger threat.
Red Ball 4.controls: Desktop: Use the left and right arrow keys or A and D to move. Press Up or W to jump.

intro: Subway Surfers is the endless runner that made lane-dodging mainstream: you play a graffiti artist being chased by an inspector and his dog after being caught tagging a train yard, sprinting down the tracks while dodging oncoming trains, barriers, and tunnels. It's a three-lane runner at its core, but the constant train traffic coming from both directions is what makes it distinct from other runners in the genre.

The loop is simple to describe and hard to master: swipe (or press arrow keys) to switch lanes, jump onto and over train cars, roll under barriers, and use the hoverboard when you have one to survive a single crash instead of ending the run. Coins scattered along the track let you unlock characters and boards, and power-ups like the jetpack, sneakers, or coin magnet temporarily change how you have to read the track. Score climbs the longer you survive and the more coins you grab along the way.

Mechanically the game leans on lane reading more than raw reflexes. Trains often run in parallel on multiple lanes at once, so the real skill is scanning two or three lanes ahead and deciding your route early rather than reacting at the last second. Jumping onto a train roof is often safer than staying on the ground when a barrier and a train arrive at the same time, and rolling has a brief recovery window where you can't immediately jump again, which catches new players off guard.

A genuinely useful habit is to treat the hoverboard as a save rather than something to activate on cooldown — it absorbs one hit, so it's most valuable right when the track gets chaotic (multiple trains merging, a sudden barrier after a jump) rather than burned early for safety. Coin magnets and score multipliers are worth prioritizing over jetpacks if your goal is a high score rather than just surviving, since they stack value across the whole run instead of one brief window.

Subway Surfers also refreshes its map periodically with different city themes, which changes scenery but keeps the core dodge-and-collect loop identical, so skills you build in one city carry over directly to the next.
Subway Surfers.howTo: Switch lanes with the left and right arrow keys, jump over obstacles and onto train roofs with the up arrow, and slide under barriers with the down arrow. Watch two lanes ahead rather than the obstacle directly in front of you, save power-ups for genuinely dangerous stretches, and prioritize a clear lane over grabbing every coin.

intro: Slope is one long fall. You steer a ball down a neon course that keeps tilting away beneath you, and you have exactly two inputs: left and right. There is no jump, no brake and no checkpoint. A run lasts until you clip a red block or miss the track entirely, and then it begins again at zero.

The difficulty is acceleration. Speed climbs continuously for as long as you stay alive, so the course is not really getting harder — your reaction window is getting shorter. The same gap you drifted through comfortably at the start becomes something you have to commit to a full second early, and steering inputs that felt gentle begin to throw you off the edge.

Your score is distance, which makes every run directly comparable to the last one. The build guards that number: it saves through Unity's ObscuredPrefs, an anti-cheat wrapper that stops the stored high score being edited locally. Slope was published by Y8.
Slope.howTo: Steer in short taps rather than holding a direction, because at speed a held input turns into a much bigger movement than you intended. Favour the middle of the track when you are not actively avoiding something, so you have room to correct in either direction. Look at the far end of the course rather than at the ball — by the time an obstacle is near the ball, the decision about it has already been made.
Slope.controls: Desktop: Use the left and right arrow keys or A and D to steer.

intro: Slope 2 Player takes the one-way neon fall of Slope and puts two balls on the track at once. Each player steers their own ball down a tilting course with just left and right, and a run ends when you clip a red block or roll off the edge. Speed keeps climbing for as long as you survive, so a calm start turns into a test of nerve within seconds.

The second player changes how you play. You are no longer only chasing your own best distance — you are racing someone sitting next to you, and every crash is public. Because it is built for two people on one keyboard, it works as a pass-and-play game with no accounts, lobbies or setup: load the page, pick your keys and go.

Like the original, there is no jump, no brake and no checkpoint, so the whole game is reading the course early and committing to a line. Rounds are short, which makes rematches the natural way to play.
Slope 2 Player.howTo: Steer in short taps rather than holding a direction, and keep to the middle of the track so you can correct either way. Watch your own ball, not your opponent's — glancing across to see how they are doing is how most players clip a red block. Look far down the course, since the decision about an obstacle has to be made well before it reaches the ball.
Slope 2 Player.controls: Desktop: Player 1 steers with A and D, and Player 2 steers with the left and right arrow keys. Both players share one keyboard, so sit close.

intro: Run 3 is a running game set inside a tunnel in space, and its trick is that gravity follows whatever surface you are standing on. Run onto a wall and the wall becomes the floor — the tunnel rotates around you, and the hole you were about to fall through is now something you are running along.

There is much more structure to it than the running suggests. Explore mode maps a branching route through the tunnels, Infinite mode runs forever for score, and there is a level editor built in for making your own. Cutscenes carry a surprising amount of story between the two.

The cast is the reason people stay with it. Angel, Bunny, Child, Duplicator, Gentleman, Ghost, Ice Skater, Lizard and Ninja all move differently rather than looking different — the Skater cannot stop easily, the Lizard climbs walls — and unlocking them changes which routes are viable. Crumbling and ice tiles, a currency and a long achievement list fill out the rest.
Run 3.howTo: Turn the tunnel deliberately rather than treating gaps as things to jump: stepping onto a wall to avoid a hole is the intended solution far more often than a jump is. Match the character to the route, since several passages in Explore mode are effectively impossible for one character and straightforward for another. Watch for crumbling tiles on a second pass — they are still gone from where your first attempt broke them.
Run 3.controls: Desktop: Use the arrow keys or WASD to move and jump.

intro: Tetris is the block-stacking puzzle game that most other puzzle games are measured against. Seven shapes, called tetrominoes, fall into a narrow well one at a time, and you rotate and slide each one into place. Fill a row completely and it disappears; clear four rows at once and you have scored a Tetris, which is where the biggest points are.

The rules never change, but the pressure does. The pieces fall faster as your level rises, mistakes leave gaps that are hard to reach, and the game ends when the stack touches the top. The skill is not speed so much as planning: where this piece goes matters less than where the next three will fit.
Tetris was created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov while he was working at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow, and it has since become one of the most widely ported games ever made.
Tetris.howTo: Keep your stack as flat as you can and avoid leaving holes under blocks, since a single buried gap can cost you several rows. Leave one column open at the side for the long I piece so you can clear four rows at a time. Use the next-piece preview to decide where the current piece goes, and place it before it falls too fast to think.
Tetris.controls: Desktop: In most versions, use the left and right arrow keys to move, Up to rotate, Down for a soft drop, and Space for a hard drop.

intro: 1v1.LOL is a free third-person shooter that mixes gunfights with Fortnite-style building. You place walls, ramps and floors on the fly to take high ground and block incoming shots, and you win a duel by landing more hits than your opponent while keeping your own structures standing.

The game offers several modes: 1v1 duels, battle royale, team modes such as 2v2, box fights in a small enclosed arena, and a practice mode for building without combat. That makes it easy to sharpen one skill at a time before you jump into a real match.
1v1.LOL was made by the studio JustPlay.LOL and is playable in a browser as well as on mobile. Matches are short, which is why it is so easy to go for one more round.
1v1 Lol.howTo: Build first and shoot second: a wall in front of you buys time, and a ramp gets you above your opponent, where the shot is easier. Keep moving while you shoot instead of standing still behind your walls. If your version has a building practice or aim training mode, spend a few minutes there before ranked-style matches, because building speed is the skill that improves fastest with practice.

intro: Tiny Fishing is an idle-style fishing game with a very simple loop: cast your line, let the hook sink, then reel it back up and collect every fish you touch on the way. Each catch pays out money, and the money goes straight back into your next run.

Money you earn buys new stock, bigger shelves and monkey workers who take over jobs for you, and the store expands into new marts. There are six marts in total, each with its own layout and product, starting with bananas and moving on to chocolate bars, chocolate muffins, fish, apples and coconut drinks. It was made by the independent developer TinyDobbins.
Monkey Mart.howTo: Don't let any shelf run empty, because customers leave if they can't find what they want. Spend early earnings on stock and shelf upgrades first, then on workers so your jobs run automatically. Keep moving between crops, shelves and the checkout instead of waiting at one spot.
Monkey Mart.controls: Desktop: Use the arrow keys or WASD to move your monkey, and walk up to crops, shelves and the checkout to work. Touch screens: drag on the screen to move.

intro: Eggy Car is a physics driving game where an egg sits loose on top of your car, and your only job is to drive as far as you can without dropping it. The road is a series of hills, valleys and bumps, and every one of them can send the egg flying. If it breaks, the run is over.

Speed doesn't help much here. Patience, balance and careful throttle control matter more, and the game has no timer, so you can take your time. Coins you collect unlock new vehicles that handle the egg differently, from the free starter car to heavier ones such as the Eggy Truck, and power-ups like Freeze temporarily hold the egg in place. It was made by Beedo Games.
Eggy Car.howTo: Watch the egg, not the car, since the egg shows you what is about to go wrong. Ease off the gas and let gravity carry you down slopes, and use short bursts of throttle to climb. Don't brake suddenly, because a hard stop sends the egg forward.
Eggy Car.controls: Desktop: Right arrow or D to accelerate, and left arrow or A to brake and reverse. Touch screens: tap the gas pedal on the right or the brake pedal on the left.

intro: Stacktris is a physics-based take on Tetris. Instead of dropping blocks into a tidy well and clearing rows, you stack tetrominoes, the same four-square shapes from Tetris, onto a small platform and try to build the tallest tower you can. Nothing disappears, so every piece you place stays in the tower and has to stay balanced.

That changes the puzzle completely. A piece that looks like a perfect fit can still tip, slide or knock the pieces beneath it, so the challenge is about balance and patience, not speed. Stacktris was made by Fancade, the same creator behind Drive Mad and Monster Tracks, and was released in February 2023.
Stacktris.howTo: Build a wide, flat base first, and place pieces flat side down whenever you can. Avoid leaving gaps that the next piece will rest on unevenly, and use the long pieces to span across, not to build tall and narrow. Take your time, because there is no rush, and it is better to wait for a piece to settle than to add another on top of a wobble.
Stacktris.controls: Desktop: Use the mouse or the keys shown in the game to move and rotate each piece, then drop it into place. Touch screens: use the on-screen controls or drag the piece.
